title: Joshua 7:1–5
context: Joshua 7 follows directly on the fall of Jericho, where the city was “devoted” to the LORD and Israel was warned to “keep yourselves from what is devoted to destruction” (6:17–18). The Hebrew term behind “devoted” (herem) marks something set apart wholly to the LORD, either destroyed or, for metals, given to his treasury (6:19, 24). Chapter 7 opens by telling the reader what Joshua does not yet know: Achan has taken some of the devoted things, and the LORD’s anger burns against Israel as a whole. Verses 2–5 then narrate the first attack on Ai, planned on human confidence and ending in defeat, with the people’s hearts melting as the Canaanites’ hearts once had (2:11; 5:1).

verses.text: But the children of Israel committed a trespass in the devoted things; for Achan, the son of Carmi, the son of Zabdi, the son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah, took some of the devoted things. Therefore the LORD’s anger burned against the children of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: The narrator names the individual, Achan, with a full genealogy reaching back to Judah, yet says “the children of Israel committed a trespass.” One man’s act is counted as Israel’s breach. Arminian readers stress that Achan acted freely against a clear command (6:18), and that his choice had real consequences for the whole people. Covenant life is a genuine relationship in which human faithfulness and unfaithfulness matter.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see here the covenant solidarity of God’s people: Israel stands before God as one body, so the sin of a member implicates the whole until it is dealt with (compare 22:20, “That man didn’t perish alone in his iniquity”). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as teaching that God is holy, that sin is never merely private within the covenant community, and that his anger is a real response to real transgression.

verses.text: Joshua sent men from Jericho to Ai, which is beside Beth Aven, on the east side of Bethel, and spoke to them, saying, “Go up and spy out the land.” The men went up and spied out Ai.
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua repeats the method used at Jericho (2:1) and sends spies, this time to Ai, “beside Beth Aven, on the east side of Bethel.” Nothing in the verse records Joshua seeking the LORD before the attack, unlike the explicit divine instructions that framed Jericho (6:2–5). Arminian readers note the contrast as a warning about drifting into self-reliance after success, a danger every believer faces.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the absence of any word from the LORD here, especially set beside 8:1, where the LORD himself initiates and directs the renewed attack. The narrative quietly teaches that victory belongs to God’s word and presence, not to sound tactics alone. Shared ground: both traditions read the episode as a lesson that past blessing is no substitute for present dependence on God.

verses.text: They returned to Joshua, and said to him, “Don’t let all the people go up, but let about two or three thousand men go up and strike Ai. Don’t make all the people to toil there, for there are only a few of them.”
verses.arminianNotes: The spies’ report is confident: only “two or three thousand men” are needed, “for there are only a few of them.” Their assessment is purely military. Arminian readers observe that the report is not wicked in itself, but it reckons without the hidden breach of 7:1. Israel’s strength was never its numbers but the LORD’s presence, which human calculation cannot measure or assume.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the irony that the spies count the enemy accurately while being blind to the real problem within Israel’s own camp. Strength is measured by God’s favor, and that favor has been forfeited for the moment by covenant breach. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as exposing overconfidence and as preparing the reader for the reversal that follows in verses 4–5.

verses.text: So about three thousand men of the people went up there, and they fled before the men of Ai.
verses.arminianNotes: About three thousand men go up, and they flee “before the men of Ai.” The phrasing reverses the pattern promised in the conquest, where enemies would flee before Israel. Arminian readers stress that covenant blessing in the land was conditioned on obedience (compare 1:8), so the defeat is the outworking of a real breach, not an arbitrary turn of fortune.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s hand in the defeat as much as in the victory at Jericho. The LORD who fought for Israel now withholds his help, as 7:12 will explain, because the devoted thing is among them. Shared ground: both traditions agree the defeat is covenant discipline, a judgment that exposes sin and calls the people back, rather than a sign that God has abandoned his promise.

verses.text: The men of Ai struck about thirty-six men of them. They chased them from before the gate even to Shebarim, and struck them at the descent. The hearts of the people melted, and became like water.
verses.arminianNotes: The losses, “about thirty-six men,” are small in number yet devastating in effect: “The hearts of the people melted, and became like water.” The same melting had described the Canaanites’ fear of Israel (2:11; 5:1). Arminian readers note how quickly confidence can collapse when God’s presence is withdrawn, and that the loss of real lives shows the cost of one person’s hidden sin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the reversed imagery a sign that Israel’s courage was always derived from God, not native to the nation. When he withdraws his help, Israel is no different from the peoples it was sent to dispossess. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse soberly, honoring the thirty-six who died, and see it as the turning point that drives Joshua to seek the LORD in verses 6–9.
